endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
endorsements.quote: Conduct AI red-teaming to assess issues such as: Outputting of training data samples, and subsequent reverse engineering, model extraction, and membership inference risks; Revealing biometric, confidential, copyrighted, licensed, patented, personal, proprietary, sensitive, or trade-marked information; Tracking or revealing location information of users or members of training datasets.

endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: This step includes assessing whether counterfactual tests are conducted both with and without relevant sociodemographic subgroups in order to evaluate AI model performance.

endorsements.title: Framework for bias evaluation in large language models in healthcare settings
endorsements.quote: The experimental design will systematically alter the vignettes’ attributes.

endorsements.title: Challenges of Implementing LLMs in Clinical Practice: Perspectives
endorsements.quote: This stresses the need for bias evaluation and mitigation before deploying LLM-based decision support tools.

endorsements.title: From prediction to intervention: causal digital twins for personalized clinical decision support
endorsements.quote: Fair models should not amplify existing inequities or underperform for marginalized populations.

endorsements.title: The Ethics of Leveraging Routinely Collected Patient Data for AI Development: Mixed Methods Study
endorsements.quote: Conduct fairness audits to explicitly assess whether model outputs are biased by demographic differences or by specific clinical routines and documentation practices that vary across institutions.

endorsements.title: Centering the marginalized: AI-driven strategies for advancing health equity in rare disease care
endorsements.quote: Equity-centered evaluation metrics should include (1) stratified and worst-group performance reporting, 55 (2) disparity-aware error metrics, 56 (3) counterfactual and robustness-based evaluations when subgroup sizes are small, and (4) longitudinal and deployment-level indicators of equity impact.

evidence.title: MedVoiceBias: A Controlled Study of Audio LLM Behavior in Clinical Decision-Making
evidence.outcome: Audio LLM surgical recommendations varying by voice age, gender, emotion versus identical text inputs
evidence.effect: Surgical recommendations for audio varied by up to 35% versus text; age disparities up to 12% between young and elderly voices, persisting in most models despite chain-of-thought prompting.
evidence.quote: Further analysis uncovered age disparities of up to 12% between young and elderly voices, which persisted in most models despite chain-of-thought prompting.
evidence.sample_unit: clinical cases (each synthesized with 36 voice profiles)

evidence.title: Auditing Sex/Gender Disparities in Emergency Triage with LLM-based Paired Comparisons
evidence.outcome: Change in predicted triage severity when only patient sex is flipped in otherwise identical records
evidence.effect: Sex-swapped pairs were more likely to get a lower-severity score as female than male: 1.1% (95% CI 0.9-1.3) in the French cohort, 2.2% (1.7-2.7) in MIMIC-IV.
evidence.quote: Fine-tuning Mistral NeMo 12B for triage prediction and using Mistral Small 24B for pair generation, we find otherwise identical presentations were more likely to receive a lower-severity predicted score as female than male: 1.1% (95% CI 0.9-1.3) in the French cohort, 2.2% (1.7-2.7) in MIMIC-IV.
evidence.sample_unit: emergency department admissions (French cohort, more than 140,000)

evidence.title: Socioeconomic Inference in LLM Medical Triage: Same Symptoms, Different ZIP Code
evidence.outcome: ER referral rate changes when only patient SES signal varied in prompts
evidence.effect: All three models raised ER referral for lower-SES patients given explicit signal (spreads 13-50 points); Gemini shifted 11.4 points pooled from ZIP code alone (p=1.4e-7); Claude -0.1; GPT-5.4-mini 2.0.
evidence.quote: All three models raise their emergency-room (ER) referral rate for lower-SES patients given the explicit signal (spreads of 13-50 percentage points).
evidence.sample_unit: simulated triage queries (single fixed symptom vignette with varied SES signals)

evidence.title: Counterfactual Fairness Audits of Multi-Step Clinical LLM Agents Require a Measured Per-Action Instability Floor
evidence.outcome: Counterfactual demographic flip rates versus run-to-run instability floor
evidence.effect: No demographic contrast was distinguishable from the 8.7% instability floor; counterfactual flip rates uninterpretable without a per-action floor. Majority vote over five draws removed 39% of the floor.
evidence.quote: No demographic contrast in our data was distinguishable from that floor.

evidence.title: Evaluation of Gender Bias in the Evaluation of Synthetic Cardiovascular Disease Cases with Open Source LLMs
evidence.outcome: Change in LLM cardiovascular ratings when only patient gender varied in identical vignettes
evidence.effect: Minimal gender differences; only Gemma-2b diagnostic certainty differed for female patients (58% vs 48%, p=0.031, adjusted p=0.092). Effect sizes small (Cohen's h 0.01-0.18).
evidence.quote: Only one statistically significant finding emerged: Gemma-2b assigned higher diagnostic certainty to female patients in initial presentations (58% vs. 48%, p=0.031, adjusted p=0.092).
evidence.sample_unit: model responses (500 synthetic cases x 3 models)

evidence.title: New Model, Old Risks? Sociodemographic Bias and Adversarial Hallucinations Vulnerability in GPT-5
evidence.outcome: Mental-health screening by label
evidence.effect: Several LGBTQIA+ labels were flagged in 100% of cases versus ~41–73% for comparable groups with GPT-4o.
evidence.quote: Notably, several LGBTQIA+ labels were flagged for mental-health screening in 100% of cases, versus ~41–73% for comparable groups with GPT-4o.
evidence.sample_unit: physician-validated emergency vignettes (each replayed across 32 sociodemographic labels plus control)

evidence.title: Asymmetric sociodemographic disparity in evidence-grounded clinical AI
evidence.outcome: Change in AI mental-health screening recommendations when sociodemographic labels were varied in identical cases
evidence.effect: OE flagged many historically marginalized groups 3-10 times more often than unmarked cases; unhoused 78-87% vs 9% control; transgender 22-24%; Black transgender women 47%.
evidence.quote: OE was consistent on the codified clinical decisions, triage, workup, and treatment, but diverged sharply on mental-health screening, where it flagged many historically marginalized groups between three and ten times more often than demographically unmarked cases.
evidence.sample_unit: emergency-department cases (each varied across 20 sociodemographic labels)

evidence.title: A case report on gendered biases in a Finnish healthcare AI assistant
evidence.outcome: Output differences across male, female, and gender-neutral variants of identical clinical queries
evidence.effect: Substantial, clinically significant differences across gendered variants, including differential treatment urgency, inappropriate symptom associations, and misidentified clinical context; female variants framed around childcare and reproductive health.
evidence.quote: We observed substantial and clinically significant differences across gendered variants, including differential treatment urgency, inappropriate symptom associations, and misidentification of clinical context.
evidence.sample_unit: clinical queries (each in three gendered variants)

evidence.title: Coding Inequity: Assessing GPT-4’s Potential for Perpetuating Racial and Gender Biases in Healthcare
evidence.outcome: Change in GPT-4 diagnoses and plans when patient race/ethnicity/gender varied in standardized vignettes
evidence.effect: Differential diagnoses were more likely to include stereotyping diagnoses; plans showed significant association between demographics and recommendations for more expensive procedures and differences in patient perception.
evidence.quote: Assessment and plans created by the model showed significant association between demographic attributes and recommendations for more expensive procedures as well as differences in patient perception.
evidence.sample_unit: GPT-4 generated outputs (vignettes, differential diagnoses, treatment plans) across demographic variations

evidence.title: ChatGPT Exhibits Gender and Racial Biases in Acute Coronary Syndrome Management
evidence.outcome: Guideline-concordant ACS management recommendations when varying patient gender and race in prompts
evidence.effect: Specifying patients as female, African American, or Hispanic decreased guideline-recommended medical management, diagnosis, and symptom management; largest disparities in angiography/stress testing and high-intensity statins.
evidence.quote: We find that specifying patients as female, African American, or Hispanic resulted in a decrease in guideline recommended medical management, diagnosis, and symptom management of ACS.

evidence.title: ChatGPT Influence on Medical Decision-Making, Bias, and Equity: A Randomized Study of Clinicians Evaluating Clinical Vignettes
evidence.outcome: Whether AI-assisted decisions differed by patient race and gender in randomized vignettes
evidence.effect: Physician decision accuracy improved significantly with GPT-4 advice without introducing or exacerbating existing race or gender biases (abstract-level result; no numbers given in the text).
evidence.quote: Results showed that physicians are willing to change their initial clinical impressions given AI assistance, and that this led to a significant improvement in clinical decision-making accuracy in a chest pain evaluation scenario without introducing or exacerbating existing race or gender biases.

evidence.title: Large language models to identify social determinants of health in electronic health records
evidence.outcome: Change in model predictions when race/ethnicity and gender descriptors were added to text
evidence.effect: Fine-tuned models were less likely than ChatGPT to change predictions when race/ethnicity and gender descriptors were added, suggesting less algorithmic bias (p < 0.05).
evidence.quote: Fine-tuned models were less likely than ChatGPT to change their prediction when race/ethnicity and gender descriptors were added to the text, suggesting less algorithmic bias (p < 0.05).

evidence.title: Clinical decision support for bipolar depression using large language models
evidence.venue: Neuropsychopharmacology : official publication of the American College of Neuropsychopharmacology
evidence.outcome: Change in model treatment selection when vignette gender and race were permuted
evidence.effect: Augmented model performance differed modestly across gender-race pairs (p=0.02); Black women significantly poorer than white men (Bonferroni p=0.03); base model showed no significant differences (p=0.17).
evidence.quote: In post-hoc pairwise contrasts using McNemar’s test, model performance in Black women was significantly poorer than white men (Bonferroni-corrected p = 0.03).
evidence.sample_unit: clinical vignettes (each run 20 times, 1000 model outputs per condition)

evidence.title: Even with ChatGPT, race matters
evidence.outcome: Readability of simplified radiology reports when patient race stated in prompt
evidence.effect: Statistically significant reading-grade-level differences by racial context in both ChatGPT-3.5 and ChatGPT-4; e.g., GPT-3.5 output for White and Asian was at a higher grade level than for Black or American Indian/Alaska Native.
evidence.quote: For ChatGPT-3.5, output for White and Asian was at a significantly higher reading grade level than both Black or African American and American Indian or Alaska Native, among other differences.

evidence.title: Mixed methods assessment of the influence of demographics on medical advice of ChatGPT
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
evidence.outcome: Change in diagnostic accuracy and advice when varying patient age, sex, and race/ethnicity in prompts
evidence.effect: Diagnostic accuracy not significantly different across demographic groups; urgent care recommendations and demographic tailoring appeared significantly more for 75-year-olds vs 25-year-olds (P<.01), not across race/ethnicity or sex.
evidence.quote: ChatGPT's urgent care recommendations and demographic tailoring were presented significantly more to 75-year-olds versus 25-year-olds (P < .01) but were not statistically different among race/ethnicity and sex groups.

evidence.title: Large language models improve the identification of emergency department visits for symptomatic kidney stones
evidence.outcome: Change in LLM predictions when race and gender were varied in prompts
evidence.effect: GPT-4 exhibited no racial or gender disparities, whereas GPT-3.5 failed to effectively model racial diversity.
evidence.quote: Bias assessment found that GPT-4 exhibited no racial or gender disparities, in contrast to GPT-3.5, which failed to effectively model racial diversity.

evidence.title: Exploring Biases of Large Language Models in the Field of Mental Health: Comparative Questionnaire Study of the Effect of Gender and Sexual Orientation in Anorexia Nervosa and Bulimia Nervosa Case Vignettes
evidence.outcome: Change in LLM-generated RAND-36 and EDE-Q scores when vignette gender and sexual orientation were varied
evidence.effect: ChatGPT-4 RAND-36 mental composite differed by gender (male 12.8 vs female 15.1; 95% CI -6.15 to -0.35; P=.04); no gender or sexual orientation effects on EDE-Q overall score.
evidence.quote: LLM-generated mental HRQoL estimates for AN and BN case vignettes may be biased by gender, with male cases scoring lower despite no real-world evidence supporting this pattern.
evidence.sample_unit: LLM-generated questionnaire responses (ChatGPT-4 observations from 120 vignettes, each run thrice)

evidence.title: Racial bias in AI-mediated psychiatric diagnosis and treatment: a qualitative comparison of four large language models
evidence.outcome: Bias in LLM diagnostic and treatment outputs when patient race was neutral, implied, or explicit
evidence.effect: LLMs often proposed inferior treatments when race was explicitly or implicitly indicated; diagnostic decisions showed minimal bias. NewMes-15 showed most bias, Gemini least.
evidence.quote: Results indicated that LLMs often proposed inferior treatments when patient race was explicitly or implicitly indicated, though diagnostic decisions demonstrated minimal bias.
evidence.sample_unit: LLM outputs (10 cases x 3 conditions x 4 models)

evidence.title: Clinical decision support for pharmacologic management of treatment-resistant depression with augmented large language models
evidence.venue: Journal of mood and anxiety disorders
evidence.outcome: Change in LLM treatment rankings when vignette gender or race was permuted
evidence.effect: Results were not meaningfully different when gender or race of the vignette was permuted to examine risk for bias; optimal choice prioritized in 114/320 vignettes (35.6%).
evidence.quote: Results were not meaningfully different when gender or race of the vignette was permuted to examine risk for bias.
evidence.sample_unit: vignette evaluations (20 vignettes with gender and race permutations)

evidence.title: Detecting Sociodemographic Biases in the Content and Quality of Large Language Model-Generated Nursing Care: Cross-Sectional Simulation Study
evidence.outcome: Differences in GPT-4 care plan themes across counterfactually varied patient sociodemographic attributes
evidence.effect: Low-income profiles less likely to include Environmental Adjustment (aRR 0.90); older profiles more likely to include Pain Management (aRR 1.33) and Family Support (aRR 1.62); lower education increased Family Support (aRR 1.10).
evidence.quote: Care plans generated for low-income patient profiles were less likely to include the theme Environmental Adjustment (adjusted relative risk [aRR] 0.90).

evidence.title: Large language model bias auditing for periodontal diagnosis using an ambiguity-probe methodology: a pilot study
evidence.outcome: Change in LLM periodontal stage/grade outputs when varying sociodemographic persona attributes
evidence.effect: No statistically significant sociodemographic bias in either model after FDR correction, in clear-cut and ambiguous scenarios; errors attributed to diagnostic boundary instability rather than bias.
evidence.quote: However, a robust fairness analysis using cumulative link models with false discovery rate correction revealed no statistically significant sociodemographic bias in either model.

evidence.title: Emily vs. Lakisha: Quantifying socioeconomic and structural disparities in AI-generated ovarian cancer care plans
evidence.outcome: Change in LLM output when patient race proxy name and geography varied in vignettes
evidence.effect: Models were 16.8 times more likely (OR: 16.80) to introduce unprompted cost warnings for 'Lakisha' compared to 'Emily,' regardless of location; clinical guideline adherence remained high across demographics.
evidence.quote: Sensitivity analysis revealed that 'Financial Fixation' was driven almost exclusively by Race (p < 0.001), with models being 16.8 times more likely (OR: 16.80) to introduce unprompted cost warnings for 'Lakisha' compared to 'Emily,' regardless of location.

evidence.title: Investigation of Bias Using ChatGPT-4 in Pain Management and Patient Profiling
evidence.outcome: Whether LLM pain recommendations change when patient demographic attributes in prompts are varied
evidence.effect: Race, language, and socioeconomic status often did not alter recommendations; opioid use disorder history consistently changed suggestions (opioid-sparing). Overall agreement 82% for ED medications, 78% for discharge medications.
evidence.quote: When using cGPT, demographic factors such as race, language, and socioeconomic status often did not alter recommendations.

evidence.title: Omission and hallucination prevalence of clinical guidelines in diagnostic large language model outputs
evidence.outcome: Change in guideline omission/hallucination across varied patient sex, ethnicity, and location in vignettes
evidence.effect: Omission and hallucination rates were generally similar across sex or ethnicity but particularly sensitive to patient location; guideline citation rate ranged 0% to 78.39% across sociodemographic vignettes.
evidence.quote: Omission and hallucination rates were generally similar across vignettes with different sex or ethnicity data, yet were particularly sensitive to patient location.

evidence.title: Sociodemographic bias in large language model clinical trial screening
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
evidence.outcome: LLM trial eligibility and related-domain judgments across counterfactual sociodemographic label variants versus control
evidence.effect: Across 58 protocols and 5.3 million evaluations, eligibility judgments were largely stable across identities. Race and ethnicity had minimal effects after accounting for socioeconomic status. Homelessness produced the largest negative eligibility shift and pronounced effects in adherence, resources, and trust.
evidence.quote: Homelessness produced the largest negative eligibility shift and pronounced effects in adherence, resources, and trust.
evidence.sample_unit: LLM evaluations (58 protocols, control plus 33 identity variants, nine LLMs)

evidence.title: Implicit Gender, Racial, and Ethnic Biases in Large Language Models: An Audit Study of Automated Psychiatric Diagnoses
evidence.outcome: Change in LLM psychiatric diagnoses when patient gender and race/ethnicity cues varied with symptoms constant
evidence.effect: GPT-4o accuracy varied by gender (higher for female, lower for nonbinary); overall accuracy did not differ by race/ethnicity, but cultural bereavement and antisocial behavior were diagnosed exclusively in patients of color.
evidence.quote: Accuracy varied by gender, with higher performance for female patients and lower for nonbinary individuals.
evidence.sample_unit: LLM-generated diagnostic responses (97 DSM-5 cases x 39 demographic groups, GPT-4o analysis)

evidence.title: Assessing and mitigating demographic bias in large language models for diagnostic radiology
evidence.outcome: Significant race- or sex-related differences in LLM diagnostic accuracy under counterfactual demographic prompts
evidence.effect: Ten significant race-related and four significant sex-related differences in diagnostic accuracy were observed across models and conditions; Black patients most often had significantly lower accuracy (4/10 race comparisons).
evidence.quote: Across models and conditions, ten significant race-related and four significant sex-related differences in diagnostic accuracy were observed.

evidence.title: Disparities in AI-Based Prior Authorization for Head and Neck Reconstruction: A Large Language Model Analysis
evidence.venue: World journal of otorhinolaryngology - head and neck surgery
evidence.outcome: LLM reconstruction approval decisions varied by counterfactual patient sociodemographic attributes
evidence.effect: RFFF approved more for younger, Asian, white, high-income/high-SES patients (p<0.0001); older, Black, Hispanic, lower-income, or substance-use patients less likely to get RFFF (p<0.0001), across 19,900 simulations.
evidence.quote: Older, Black, and Hispanic patients, and those from lower-income areas or with substance use histories, were less likely to receive RFFF authorization (p < 0.0001).

evidence.title: Sociodemographic bias in LLMs' clinical decision-making for dizziness
evidence.venue: Journal of vestibular research : equilibrium & orientation
evidence.outcome: LLM recommendation shifts versus neutral control when patient sociodemographic descriptors varied
evidence.effect: Descriptors changed recommendations; mental health referral lower for Black transgender women (-12.2 pp; 95% CI -14.0 to -10.3), Black homeless patients (-9.1 pp), homeless patients (-7.7 pp); low-income neuroimaging +4.0 pp.
evidence.quote: Referral likelihood was lower for Black transgender women (-12.2 pp; 95% CI -14.0 to -10.3), Black patients experiencing homelessness (-9.1 pp; -11.0 to -7.3), and patients experiencing homelessness (-7.7 pp; -9.5 to -5.9).

evidence.title: AI-assisted rheumatology triage changes with referral framing
evidence.outcome: Change in AI triage concordance when patient race/ethnicity, socioeconomic status, and language barrier were varied
evidence.effect: Race or ethnicity, socioeconomic status, and language barrier produced no detectable effect, including in mixed-effects models accounting for repeated vignette use; framing cues (anxious, anchoring) did shift outputs.
evidence.quote: In contrast, race or ethnicity, socioeconomic status, and language barrier produced no detectable effect, including in mixed-effects models that accounted for repeated vignette use.
evidence.sample_unit: case variants (30 physician-authored rheumatology vignettes, each rephrased three times)

evidence.title: Can Large Language Models Preserve Diagnostic Accuracy Despite Patient Self-Diagnosis and Framing Bias in Hypothetical Upper-Extremity Scenarios?
evidence.outcome: Change in LLM diagnosis when randomized patient characteristics and self-diagnosis were varied
evidence.effect: Accuracy unaffected by self-diagnosis; model deviated from patient's diagnosis in 117 scenarios (65%), 104 (89%) aligned with intended diagnosis.
evidence.quote: The model deviated from the patient's proposed diagnosis in 117 scenarios (65%), of which 104 deviations (89%) appropriately aligned with the intended diagnosis.

evidence.title: OpenEvidence errs on the safe side in a structured test of triage recommendations
evidence.outcome: Change in triage recommendations when demographic and contextual modifiers varied in prompts
evidence.effect: Anchoring statements did not alter recommendations (OR = 1.08, 95% CI 0.62-1.88; Holm-adjusted p = 1.0).
evidence.quote: Anchoring statements did not alter recommendations (OR = 1.08, 95 % CI 0.62-1.88; Holm-adjusted p = 1.0).

evidence.title: Algorithmic fairness in AI-based fitness advice: evaluating socioeconomic bias in county-contextualized physical activity prescriptions
evidence.outcome: counterfactual SES audit detection
evidence.effect: Matched counterfactual audit found raw high-minus-low access-cost proxy gap of 0.306.
evidence.quote: For RQ1, the matched comparisons reveal systematic variation in coded resource assumptions across county-SES contexts: under the raw condition, the high-minus-low access-cost proxy gap is 0.306 even though represented health need is held constant.
evidence.sample_unit: synthetic patient profiles (432 scored recommendation records in full DeepSeek audit)

evidence.title: Implicit Bias in Large Language Model Diagnosis of Eating Disorders: Experimental Vignette Study
evidence.outcome: Change in LLM diagnosis when patient demographics varied in matched-pair vignettes
evidence.effect: Black patients OR 6.09 (95% CI 5.13-7.24) and Latine patients OR 9.57 (8.00-11.45) for MDD vs White; Asian patients OR 2.88 for AN; female patients OR 0.43 for AN vs males.
evidence.quote: Mixed-effects logistic regression with LLM as a random intercept revealed significant demographic biases: Black patients were over 6 times more likely to receive a major depressive disorder (MDD) diagnosis than White patients with identical presentations (odds ratio [OR] 6.09, 95% CI 5.13-7.24), Latine patients were over 9 times more likely (OR 9.57, 95% CI 8.00-11.45), and Asian patients were nearly 3 times more likely to receive an AN diagnosis (OR 2.88, 95% CI 2.44-3.42).

evidence.title: Social Status and Clinical Resource Allocation by a Large Language Model: An Evaluation of 30,618 Decisions
evidence.outcome: Change in LLM allocation choices when non-clinical patient attributes varied counterfactually with clinical need held constant
evidence.effect: Indigenous OR 16.48 and Black OR 8.07 vs White; high-status occupation OR 0.064; friend of leadership OR 0.121; major donor OR 0.092; choice-score concordance 95.1%.
evidence.quote: Indigenous and Black race were associated with substantially higher odds of selection relative to White race (Indigenous: OR 16.48, 95% CI 14.85-18.28; Black: OR 8.07, 95% CI 7.32-8.90), corresponding to position-balanced absolute increases in selection probability of 30.7 and 16.3 percentage points, respectively.

evidence.title: MEDEQUALQA: Evaluating Biases in LLMs with Counterfactual Reasoning
evidence.outcome: Stability of GPT-4.1 reasoning traces across counterfactual pronoun variants (STS)
evidence.effect: Overall high similarity (mean STS >0.80), but consistent localized divergences in cited risk factors, guideline anchors, and differential ordering, even when final diagnoses remain unchanged.
evidence.quote: Our results show overall high similarity (mean STS >0.80), but reveal consistent localized divergences in cited risk factors, guideline anchors, and differential ordering, even when final diagnoses remain unchanged.
evidence.sample_unit: benchmark items (counterfactual vignette ablations, ~23,000 per pronoun variant)

evidence.title: BioPulse-QA: A Dynamic Biomedical Question-Answering Benchmark for Evaluating Factuality, Robustness, and Bias in Large Language Models
evidence.outcome: LLM output differences when demographic attributes are varied in questions
evidence.effect: Bias testing showed negligible differences across demographic variants.
evidence.quote: Performance differences are larger for paraphrasing than for typographical errors, while bias testing shows negligible differences.
evidence.sample_unit: expert-verified question-answer pairs and perturbed variants

evidence.title: Counterfactual Cultural Cues Reduce Medical QA Accuracy in LLMs: Identifier vs Context Effects
evidence.outcome: Accuracy change when culture-related identifiers/context are inserted into otherwise invariant medical questions
evidence.effect: Cultural cues significantly affect accuracy (Cochran's Q, p<10^-14), with largest degradation when identifier and context co-occur (up to 3-7 percentage points under option-only prompting); neutral edits produce smaller, non-systematic changes.
evidence.quote: Across models, cultural cues significantly affect accuracy (Cochran's Q, $p<10^-14$), with the largest degradation when identifier and context co-occur (up to 3-7 percentage points under option-only prompting), while neutral edits produce smaller, non-systematic changes.

evidence.title: First, Do No Harm (With LLMs): Mitigating Racial Bias via Agentic Workflows
evidence.outcome: Racial bias in differential diagnosis ranking across race-varied prompts, standalone vs agentic workflow
evidence.effect: DeepSeek V3 in an agentic workflow improved 0.0348 in mean p-value, 0.1166 in median p-value, and 0.0949 in mean difference versus standalone, though not uniform across every metric.
evidence.quote: When embedded in an agentic workflow, DeepSeek V3 showed an improvement of 0.0348 in mean p-value, 0.1166 in median p-value, and 0.0949 in mean difference relative to the standalone model, although improvement was not uniform across every metric.
evidence.sample_unit: LLM-generated synthetic cases and differential diagnosis lists

evidence.title: EQUITRIAGE: A Fairness Audit of Gender Bias in LLM-Based Emergency Department Triage
evidence.outcome: Change in ESI assignment under gender-swapped counterfactual vignettes (flip rate, F/M undertriage ratio)
evidence.effect: All five models exceeded the pre-registered 5% flip threshold (9.9% to 43.8%); DeepSeek F/M 2.15:1 and Gemini 1.34:1 directional female undertriage.
evidence.quote: All five models produced flip rates above a pre-registered 5% threshold (9.9% to 43.8%).

evidence.title: Mitigating the risk of health inequity exacerbated by large language models
evidence.outcome: LLM output changes when non-decisive socio-demographic factors are added to inputs; EquityGuard detection and mitigation
evidence.effect: Adding non-decisive socio-demographic factors (race, sex, income, LGBT+ status, homelessness, illiteracy, disability, unemployment) led to incorrect and harmful outputs. EquityGuard was reported effective in promoting equitable outcomes; no numbers given in the abstract.
evidence.quote: However, our study shows that incorporating non-decisive socio-demographic factors, such as race, sex, income level, LGBT+ status, homelessness, illiteracy, disability, and unemployment, into the input of LLMs can lead to incorrect and harmful outputs.

evidence.title: Comparative Analysis of LLMs in Dry Eye Syndrome Healthcare Information
evidence.outcome: Change in LLM dry eye responses when patient race and sex varied in prompts
evidence.effect: Cultural sensitivity scores varied by model and demographic: Grok scored 3 for Black and Hispanic demographics, Meta AI showed minimal cultural tailoring (0.5 ± 0.5). All models recommended specialist consultation.
evidence.quote: Cultural sensitivity scores revealed Grok demonstrated highest awareness for minority populations (scoring 3 for Black and Hispanic demographics), while Meta AI showed minimal cultural tailoring (0.5 ± 0.5).

evidence.title: Generative pre-trained transformer reinforces historical gender bias in diagnosing women's cardiovascular symptoms
evidence.outcome: Change in GPT-4o differential diagnosis accuracy when patient gender was swapped in real notes
evidence.effect: Significant diagnostic accuracy differences in 11 of 50 cases (22%); female patients scored lower for coronary artery disease (P<0.01), abdominal aortic aneurysm (P<1.0×10^-9), atrial fibrillation (P<0.01).
evidence.quote: Diagnostic accuracy across genders was determined by comparing model outputs to actual discharge diagnoses via FDR-corrected Mann-Whitney U tests, revealing significant diagnostic accuracy differences in 11 cases (22%).
evidence.sample_unit: de-identified cardiovascular patient notes (gender-swapped; 10,000 prompts) plus 15,000 simulated cases per model

evidence.title: Bias Patterns in the Application of LLMs for Clinical Decision Support: A Comprehensive Study
evidence.outcome: Output disparities when patient demographic attributes varied in clinical vignette prompts across eight LLMs
evidence.effect: Counterfactual demographic red-teaming revealed various disparities across protected groups; larger models were not necessarily less biased and medical fine-tuning did not consistently outperform general-purpose models.
evidence.quote: Our experiments reveal various disparities across protected groups.

evidence.title: Demographic prompt cues shift clinical recommendations in multimodal large language models: a multi-model audit of 25,380 dental radiograph assessments
evidence.outcome: Change in LLM clinical recommendations when patient race/ethnicity and sex cues varied in prompts
evidence.effect: All three models altered recommendations with demographic cues; Claude showed significant race effects (p<.001); GPT-5.4 Hispanic invasiveness β=+0.052; Gemini Black invasiveness β=+0.026; all shifts <6% of one category width.
evidence.quote: All three models altered recommendations when demographic cues were introduced.
evidence.sample_unit: API calls (705 panoramic radiographs x 12 conditions x 3 models)

evidence.title: Large language models perpetuate bias in palliative care: Development and analysis of the Palliative Care Adversarial Dataset (PCAD)
evidence.outcome: GPT-4o response bias in paired counterfactual scenarios varying ethnicity, age, and diagnosis
evidence.effect: Pooled bias rate 0.26 (95% CI: 0.20, 0.32) across 84 paired scenarios; most frequent dimension was potential for withholding (0.25; 95% CI: 0.17, 0.34).
evidence.quote: For counterfactual scenarios, the pooled bias rate was 0.26 (95% CI: 0.20, 0.32), with "potential for withholding" as the most frequently identified dimension of bias (0.25; 95% CI: 0.17, 0.34), such as withholding interventions based on identity.
evidence.sample_unit: adversarial questions and counterfactual scenarios (100 direct questions, 84 paired scenarios)

evidence.title: Same child, different risk: demographic bias in childhood obesity attribution by large language models
evidence.outcome: Change in obesity risk attribution when child demographic attributes varied in prompts
evidence.effect: Socioeconomic status produced low-income attribution in 40/42 decisions (decision change rate 19.0%); urban-rural decision change rate 52.4%; most models attributed higher risk to Black and Hispanic/Latino children.
evidence.quote: Socioeconomic status produced the most consistent attribution pattern (low-income attribution in 40/42 decisions; decision change rate 19.0%).

evidence.title: Differences in tone of AI and care team responses to patient messages by patient demographics
evidence.outcome: Demographic differences in tone of AI-drafted patient message replies
evidence.effect: AI drafts had lower odds of polite language for Hispanic vs White patients. They had lower odds of positive affect for Hispanic, non-English-preferring, female-sex, and lower-area-income patients.
evidence.quote: AI-GDRs also had lower odds of conveying positive affect in responses to patients who were Hispanic, preferred a non-English language, assigned female sex at birth, or lived in an area with a lower average income.
evidence.sample_unit: message triads (patient message, AI-generated draft reply, care team response)

evidence.title: The Biased Oracle: Assessing LLMs' Understandability and Empathy in Medical Diagnoses
evidence.outcome: Change in LLM explanation and empathy when patient socio-demographic attributes vary
evidence.effect: LLMs adapted explanations to socio-demographic variables and patient conditions and showed biased affective empathy, producing uneven accessibility and support; no numbers given in the abstract.
evidence.quote: However, they also generate overly complex content and display biased affective empathy, leading to uneven accessibility and support.

evidence.title: MedVoiceBias: A Controlled Study of Audio LLM Behavior in Clinical Decision-Making
evidence.outcome: age-based voice disparity
evidence.effect: Age disparities of up to 12% occurred between young and elderly voices and persisted in most models despite chain-of-thought prompting.
evidence.quote: Further analysis uncovered age disparities of up to 12% between young and elderly voices, which persisted in most models despite chain-of-thought prompting.
evidence.sample_unit: clinical cases (each synthesized with 36 voice profiles)

evidence.title: Simulating Psychological Risks in Human-AI Interactions: Real-Case Informed Modeling of AI-Induced Addiction, Anorexia, Depression, Homicide, Psychosis, and Suicide
evidence.outcome: LLM response performance varying by simulated persona demographics such as age and income
evidence.effect: LLMs performed worse with elderly users but better with low- and middle-income groups compared to high-income groups.
evidence.quote: Regression analysis reveals variability across persona types: LLMs tend to perform worse with elderly users but better with low- and middle-income groups compared to high-income groups.

evidence.title: Uncovering Latent Bias in LLM-Based Emergency Department Triage Through Proxy Variables
evidence.outcome: LLM triage severity changes when patient proxy variable qualifiers (32 paired positive/negative) are varied
evidence.effect: Discriminatory behavior mediated through proxy variables in ED triage. LLMs systematically shifted perceived patient severity when specific tokens appeared, whether framed positively or negatively. No numeric results in abstract.
evidence.quote: Our results reveal discriminatory behavior mediated through proxy variables in ED triage scenarios, as well as a systematic tendency for LLMs to modify perceived patient severity when specific tokens appear in the input context, regardless of whether they are framed positively or negatively.
evidence.sample_unit: ED triage cases with paired proxy-variable qualifiers

evidence.title: Implicit Geographic Inference in LLM Medical Triage: Language-Driven Disparities in Emergency Recommendations
evidence.outcome: Change in ER recommendations when only prompt language or location attribute varied
evidence.effect: A US location sentence raised ER recommendations by up to 76.7 percentage points for non-English prompts; English prompt with Tokyo location cut ER rate from 30% to 6.7%.
evidence.quote: Adding a single sentence specifying the patient's US location increases ER recommendations by up to 76.7 percentage points for non-English prompts, while the reverse anchor (English prompt with a Tokyo location) reduces the ER rate from 30% to 6.7%.
evidence.country: Not applicable (simulated prompts in six languages; US and Tokyo locations tested)

evidence.title: Socioeconomic Inference in LLM Medical Triage: Same Symptoms, Different ZIP Code
evidence.outcome: ER referral rate variation by socioeconomic status
evidence.effect: All three models raised ER referral rates by 13-50 percentage points for lower-SES patients given explicit signals; Gemini shifted ER rates by 11.4 points based on ZIP code alone (p = 1.4e-7).
evidence.quote: All three models raise their emergency-room (ER) referral rate for lower-SES patients given the explicit signal (spreads of 13-50 percentage points).
evidence.sample_unit: simulated triage queries (single fixed symptom vignette with varied SES signals)

evidence.title: Does Splitting a Triage Decision Across Agents Hide Bias or Help Catch It? A Multi-Agent Simulation Study of LLM-Based Resource Allocation Under Audit Capacity Constraints
evidence.outcome: Rate of biased outcomes in paired cases differing only in one demographic attribute
evidence.effect: Biased outcomes occurred in 6.9% (single-agent) vs. 6.1% (nine-agent pipeline) of paired cases, p = 0.498; no measurable difference between conditions.
evidence.quote: We find no measurable difference in how often biased outcomes occur between the two conditions (6.9% vs. 6.1%, p = 0.498).

evidence.title: How Does LGBTQIA+ Identity Affect LLM Behavior? Implications for Requirements Engineering of Mental Health AI Systems
evidence.outcome: Change in ChatGPT mental health responses when patient LGBTQIA+ or straight identity is disclosed
evidence.effect: Identity disclosure did not substantially affect completeness or supportive guidance. LGBTQIA+ responses had substantially more identity acknowledgment, contextual expansion, unsupported assumptions and occasional stereotypical reasoning than the other two conditions.
evidence.quote: Our findings indicate that LGBTQIA+ identity disclosure did not substantially affect response completeness or supportive guidance.

evidence.title: Sense and Sensitivity: Benchmarking LLM Clinical Triage Recommendations with Physician Experts
evidence.outcome: Sensitivity of LLM triage recommendations to gender perturbations compared with physicians
evidence.effect: LLM recommendations were more sensitive to gender and tone perturbations than human physician recommendations.
evidence.quote: Further, we find that LLM recommendations are more sensitive to gender and tone perturbations than human recommendations.
evidence.sample_unit: clinical scenarios (over 6,000; 7,000 physician annotations; 225,000 model responses)

evidence.title: New Model, Old Risks? Sociodemographic Bias and Adversarial Hallucinations Vulnerability in GPT-5
evidence.outcome: Change in GPT-5 triage, testing, treatment, mental-health recommendations when sociodemographic labels varied
evidence.effect: GPT-5 reproduced subgroup-linked variation, with higher urgency and less advanced testing for several marginalized groups; several LGBTQIA+ labels flagged for mental-health screening in 100% of cases vs ~41–73% with GPT-4o.
evidence.quote: GPT-5 reproduced subgroup-linked variation, with higher assigned urgency and less advanced testing for several historically marginalized and intersectional groups.
evidence.sample_unit: physician-validated emergency vignettes (each replayed across 32 sociodemographic labels plus control)

evidence.title: Evaluating the Ethical and Clinical Implications of Generative AI in Patient-Centric Medical Applications
evidence.outcome: Change in model responses when patient demographic attributes were varied in queries
evidence.effect: Both GPT-4 and Med-PaLM 2 showed significant bias when demographic variations were introduced, especially race and immigration differences. No numbers reported in the abstract.
evidence.quote: It is also noticeable that both systems exhibited significant degree of bias in the same when demographical variations were introduced, especially in the case of race and immigration differences.

evidence.title: User memory teaches health consumer AI to wrap a no in agreement
evidence.outcome: Change in LLM medical recommendation when saved patient memory and preferences were added to the prompt
evidence.effect: Recommendation shifted only 1.9 to 4.0 percentage points (p=0.12 and p=0.02), while the language around it shifted substantially.
evidence.quote: In 13,176 open patient-facing responses from six frontier LLMs across 36 physician-reviewed, patient-posed supplement and wellness misinformation queries, memory shifted the recommendation by only 1.9 to 4.0 percentage points (p=0.12 and p=0.02).

evidence.title: Evaluating the AI Potential as a Safety Net for Diagnosis: A Novel Benchmark of Large Language Models in Correcting Diagnostic Errors
evidence.outcome: Stability of LLM diagnostic correction across demographic and contextual token variants
evidence.effect: Across 2,200 generated variants, stability across demographic and contextual variants was inconsistent, with some models showing spurious performance shifts based on non-clinical tokens.
evidence.quote: Stability across demographic and contextual variants was inconsistent, with some models showing spurious performance shifts based on non-clinical tokens.

evidence.title: Medical errors in large language models revealed using 1,000 synthetic clinical transcripts
evidence.outcome: Triage safety differences by patient sex across simulated demographic phenotypes
evidence.effect: GPT-5.2 triage was significantly less safe for females than males (odds ratio 3.2, 95% CI 1.4-7.1).
evidence.quote: GPT-5.2 triage was significantly less safe for females than males (odds ratio 3.2 95% CI 1.4-7.1).

evidence.title: Is it possible to vaccinate AI against bias? An exploratory study in epilepsy
evidence.outcome: Accuracy gap between high and low SES vignettes with identical clinical features
evidence.effect: Base diagnostic bias gap was 45 percentage points (high SES 58% vs. low SES 13%); treatment bias gap was 25 percentage points.
evidence.quote: For diagnosis, base accuracy was 36% (43/120), with 45 percentage point bias gap (high SES 58% vs. low SES 13%); inoculation improved accuracy to 55% (66/120) and reduced bias to 27 percentage points.

evidence.title: Auditing Large Language Model–Generated Digital Standardized Patients for Demographic Bias: A Simulation Study with HIV Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis Screening as a Tracer Condition
evidence.outcome: Demographic predictors of LLM role-play probe responses in composite versus control cases
evidence.effect: Demographics predicted 5 of 9 improvised probe responses in composite role-play and 2 under control cases; case-script and role-play effects sometimes opposed and canceled (alcohol use).
evidence.quote: Demographics predicted 5 of the 9 improvised probe responses in composite role-play, and 2 under control cases.

evidence.title: Assessing Racial and Ethnic Bias in Text Generation for Healthcare-Related Tasks by ChatGPT  1
evidence.outcome: Differences in ChatGPT output sentiment, subjectivity, and word frequency when only patient race/ethnicity or insurance was varied
evidence.effect: Mean polarity 0.14, 0.14, 0.15, 0.14 by race; subjectivity 0.46 for all; polarity and subjectivity differences not significant, but word frequency differed significantly by race and subjectivity by insurance type.
evidence.quote: The differences in polarity and subjectivity across races/ethnicities were not statistically significant.
evidence.sample_unit: deidentified EHR encounters (each run four times with race/ethnicity varied)

evidence.title: ChatGPT Exhibits Gender and Racial Biases in Acute Coronary Syndrome Management
evidence.outcome: guideline-recommended ACS management
evidence.effect: Specifying patients as female, African American, or Hispanic decreased guideline-recommended medical management, diagnosis, and symptom management.
evidence.quote: We find that specifying patients as female, African American, or Hispanic resulted in a decrease in guideline recommended medical management, diagnosis, and symptom management of ACS.

evidence.title: Socio-Demographic Modifiers Shape Large Language Models’ Ethical Decisions
evidence.outcome: Change in LLM ethical choices when patient socio-demographic modifiers were added to prompts
evidence.effect: All nine models altered responses when given socio-demographic details (p<0.001). High-income modifiers increased utilitarian choices and lowered beneficence and nonmaleficence; marginalized-group modifiers raised autonomy. No model was consistent across all scenarios.
evidence.quote: All models altered their responses when introduced with socio-demographic details (p<0.001).
evidence.sample_unit: clinical ethics scenarios (each tested with 53 socio-demographic modifiers, 10 repeats, nine LLMs; ~0.5M prompts)

evidence.title: LLM-Guided Pain Management: Examining Socio-Demographic Gaps in Cancer vs non-Cancer cases
evidence.outcome: Change in LLM opioid, anxiety, stress, risk and monitoring recommendations across 34 sociodemographic variants of identical vignettes
evidence.effect: Marginalized groups (unhoused, Black, LGBTQIA+) often received more or stronger opioid recommendations, sometimes exceeding 90% in cancer settings, despite being labeled high risk; low-income/unemployed groups had elevated risk scores yet fewer opioid recommendations.
evidence.quote: Across both cancer and non-cancer cases, historically marginalized groups—especially cases labeled as individuals who are unhoused, Black, or identify as LGBTQIA+—often received more or stronger opioid recommendations, sometimes exceeding 90% in cancer settings, despite being labeled as high risk by the same models.

evidence.title: Testing domain knowledge and risk of bias of a large-scale general artificial intelligence model in mental health
evidence.outcome: Change in model diagnostic interpretation when vignette demographics (gender, race) were systematically varied
evidence.effect: Limited evidence of demographic bias overall; some gender and racial differences in model outcomes, which mirrored real-world differential prevalence estimates.
evidence.quote: We found limited evidence of model demographic bias, although we do observe some gender and racial differences in model outcomes mirroring real-world differential prevalence estimates.

evidence.title: Assessing the potential of GPT-4 to perpetuate racial and gender biases in health care: a model evaluation study
evidence.outcome: Change in differential diagnoses and plans when patient race, ethnicity, or gender varied in vignettes
evidence.effect: Differential diagnoses were more likely to include diagnoses that stereotype certain races, ethnicities, and genders. Plans showed significant association between demographic attributes and recommendations for more expensive procedures. No numbers are given in the abstract.
evidence.quote: The differential diagnoses created by GPT-4 for standardised clinical vignettes were more likely to include diagnoses that stereotype certain races, ethnicities, and genders.

evidence.title: Clinical decision support for bipolar depression using large language models
evidence.venue: Neuropsychopharmacology : official publication of the American College of Neuropsychopharmacology
evidence.outcome: race and gender counterfactual performance differences
evidence.effect: Omnibus subgroup differences p = 0.02; Black women performed significantly poorer than white men, Bonferroni-corrected p = 0.03.
evidence.quote: In post-hoc pairwise contrasts using McNemar’s test, model performance in Black women was significantly poorer than white men (Bonferroni-corrected p = 0.03).
evidence.sample_unit: clinical vignettes (each run 20 times, 1000 model outputs per condition)

evidence.title: Dimensional Measures of Psychopathology in Children and Adolescents Using Large Language Models
evidence.outcome: Differences in LLM-extracted RDoC positive valence scores by patient race
evidence.effect: Modest but statistically significant differences in positive valence scores by race (p < .05 for Asian, Black, and Hispanic individuals).
evidence.quote: Tests for bias suggested modest but statistically significant differences in positive valence scores by race (p < .05 for Asian, Black, and Hispanic individuals).

evidence.title: Generative artificial intelligence versus clinicians: Who diagnoses multiple sclerosis faster and with greater accuracy?
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy of ChatGPT when age, sex, and race/ethnicity were varied in scripted MS conversations
evidence.effect: After MRI data were included, odds of accurate diagnosis were 4.0-fold greater for Gen Z (p=0.01). Accuracy was 68% lower in males (p=0.009) and 75% lower for White subjects than for non-White subjects (p=0.0004).
evidence.quote: Post-MRI data inclusion within GPT-3.5, the odds of an accurate diagnosis was 4.0-fold greater for Gen Z participants, relative to non-Gen Z participants (p=0.01) with the diagnostic accuracy being 68% less in males relative to females (p=0.009), and 75% less for White subjects, relative to non-White subjects (p=0.0004).
evidence.sample_unit: scripted conversations (100 real people with MS plus 529 simulated derivatives)

evidence.title: Racial, ethnic, and sex bias in large language model opioid recommendations for pain management
evidence.outcome: Change in LLM pain rating and opioid recommendations when patient race/ethnicity and sex were varied
evidence.effect: Race/ethnicity and sex did not influence pain ratings or opioid name, order, or dosage recommendations for GPT-4 or Gemini; the models differed from each other (Gemini more often rated pain severe, recommended strong opioids).
evidence.quote: Race/ethnicity and sex did not influence LLM recommendations.
evidence.sample_unit: amended patient cases per LLM (40 MIMIC-IV cases x race/ethnicity and sex combinations)

evidence.title: Fairness in AI-Driven Oncology: Investigating Racial and Gender Biases in Large Language Models
evidence.outcome: Occupation predictions (oncologist vs nurse) when varying race and gender in prompts
evidence.effect: Chatbots about two times more likely to predict Blacks and Native Americans as oncology nurses than oncologists compared to Asians (p<0.01, p<0.001); females more likely than males to be predicted as nurses (p<0.001).
evidence.quote: LLM chatbots are about two times more likely to predict Blacks and Native Americans as oncology nurses than oncologists, compared to Asians (p < 0.01 and < 0.001, respectively).

evidence.title: Gender Bias in AI's Perception of Cardiovascular Risk
evidence.outcome: GPT-4 coronary artery disease risk assessment across identical vignettes varying gender and psychiatric comorbidity
evidence.effect: Psychiatric comorbidity may influence GPT-4's coronary artery disease risk assessment among men and women; the abstract gives no numbers.
evidence.quote: Results suggest that psychiatric conditions may influence GPT-4's coronary artery disease risk assessment among men and women.

evidence.title: Impact of Demographic Modifiers on Readability of Myopia Education Materials Generated by Large Language Models
evidence.outcome: Readability (SMOG, Flesch-Kincaid, Flesch Reading Ease) of myopia education text across race, ethnicity and gender prompt modifiers
evidence.effect: No readability differences by gender, race, or ethnicity for ChatGPT or Copilot; Gemini readability differed significantly by race in the prompt (p<0.05). 150 responses analyzed.
evidence.quote: Gemini-generated responses differed significantly in their SMOG Index, Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level, and Flesch Reading Ease based on the race mentioned in the prompt (p<0.05).

evidence.title: Assessing Racial and Ethnic Bias in Text Generation by Large Language Models for Health Care-Related Tasks: Cross-Sectional Study
evidence.outcome: Differences in sentiment, subjectivity, reading ease, word frequency and entity count of LLM discharge instructions across race/ethnicity
evidence.effect: Only significant difference was entity count for GPT-4 (df=42, P=.047); post hoc pairwise tests after Bonferroni correction showed no significant differences. Four LLMs were relatively invariant to race/ethnicity.
evidence.quote: The only observed statistically significant difference between race/ethnicity groups was found in entity count (GPT-4, df=42, P=.047).

evidence.title: Sociodemographic biases in medical decision making by large language models
evidence.outcome: Change in LLM clinical recommendations when patient sociodemographic labels varied with clinical details held constant
evidence.effect: Black, unhoused, or LGBTQIA+ labeled cases were more often directed to urgent care, invasive interventions or mental health evaluations; LGBTQIA+ subgroups got mental health assessments ~6-7 times more than clinically indicated; differences persisted after multiple-hypothesis correction.
evidence.quote: Compared to both a physician-derived baseline and each model's own control case without sociodemographic identifiers, cases labeled as Black or unhoused or identifying as LGBTQIA+ were more frequently directed toward urgent care, invasive interventions or mental health evaluations.
evidence.sample_unit: emergency department cases (each in 32 sociodemographic variations; >1.7 million model outputs)

evidence.title: Inherent Bias in Large Language Models: A Random Sampling Analysis
evidence.outcome: Change in GPT-4 simulated physician choices when patient and physician demographics varied
evidence.effect: Simulated physicians favored patients with demographics similar to their own, with most pairwise comparisons significant (P<.05). Nondescript physicians favored White, male, and young patients.
evidence.quote: Overall, simulated physicians consistently demonstrated racial, gender, age, political affiliation, and sexual orientation bias in clinical decision-making.
evidence.sample_unit: simulated physician decisions (13 questions x 1000 repetitions)

evidence.title: Unveiling Public Stigma for Borderline Personality Disorder: A Comparative Study of Artificial Intelligence and Mental Health Care Providers
evidence.outcome: Differences in GAI stigma, empathy and chronicity ratings between woman and man BPD vignette characters
evidence.effect: Gender biases across GAI; Gemini showed less empathy, more negative reactions and greater stigma, especially for the woman with BPD; all GAI rated the woman's problems as more chronic than the man's.
evidence.quote: Across GAI, gender biases were found with Google Gemini showing less empathy, more negative reactions, and greater public stigma, particularly for a woman with BPD, than either ChatGPT-3.5 or ChatGPT-4.
evidence.sample_unit: mental health care practitioners in the comparison sample (number of GAI responses not reported)

evidence.title: Evaluating artificial intelligence bias in nephrology: the role of diversity, equity, and inclusion in AI-driven decision-making and ethical regulation
evidence.outcome: LLM willingness to make decisions based on potentially discriminatory sociodemographic criteria in simulated nephrology cases
evidence.effect: ChatGPT 3.5 answered all scenario questions and never refused; ChatGPT 4.0 declined in 13 (16.3%) scenarios in round one and 5 (6.3%) in round two.
evidence.quote: ChatGPT 3.5 provided a response to all scenario questions and did not refuse to make decisions under any circumstances.

evidence.title: Potential to perpetuate social biases in health care by Chinese large language models: a model evaluation study
evidence.venue: International journal for equity in health
evidence.outcome: Change in LLM diagnosis, treatment and needs outputs when patient sociodemographic attributes varied
evidence.effect: LLM referral rates were higher for minority ethnic groups and for patients without insurance or with low income; pain medications were recommended more often for males.
evidence.quote: They also showed a higher referral rate, indicating potential refusal to treat patients, for minority ethnic groups and those without insurance or living with low incomes.
evidence.sample_unit: LLM-generated outputs (cases, differential diagnosis and treatment plans, patient needs assessments)

evidence.title: Evaluating anti-LGBTQIA+ medical bias in large language models
evidence.outcome: Differences in LLM outputs between paired prompts with and without LGBTQIA+ identity terms
evidence.effect: All 4 LLMs generated inappropriate responses for both prompt types; differential bias patterns were observed, with LGBTQIA+ prompts eliciting more severe bias.
evidence.quote: Qualitatively, we observed differential bias patterns, with LGBTQIA+ prompts eliciting more severe bias.
evidence.sample_unit: prompts (pairs with and without LGBTQIA+ identity terms) across 4 LLMs

evidence.title: Designing Patient-Centered Communication Aids in Pediatric Surgery Using Large Language Models
evidence.outcome: Rated quality and demographic bias of LLM explanations when prompt patient gender and age were varied
evidence.effect: Mean possibility of demographic bias was 2.49 for GPT-4 and 2.93 for Gemini. GPT-4-turbo ratings were slightly higher for male than female patients on all measures except age-appropriateness. Gemini's gender differences were less pronounced.
evidence.quote: Ratings on all measures, with the exception of age-appropriateness, were slightly higher for responses generated for male patients as compared to female patients with GPT-4-turbo, while the gender differences were less pronounced with Gemini 1.0 Pro.
evidence.sample_unit: LLM responses (40 per model), each rated by 4 clinicians

evidence.title: Quality safety and disparity of an AI chatbot in managing chronic diseases: simulated patient experiments
evidence.outcome: Differences in AI care intensity across simulated patient age and household economic status
evidence.effect: Disparities were observed by patient age and household economic status; older and wealthier patients received more intensive care.
evidence.quote: Disparities were observed based on patient age and household economic status, with older and wealthier patients receiving more intensive care.

evidence.title: Ethical implications of using general-purpose LLMs in clinical settings: a comparative analysis of prompt engineering strategies and their impact on patient safety
evidence.venue: BMC medical informatics and decision making
evidence.outcome: Differential LLM recommendations by patient age and gender in identical presentations
evidence.effect: Age bias in 8 of 30 elderly responses (26.7%; OR 2.34, p=0.02); gender bias in 6 of 15 cardiovascular scenarios (40%), delayed cardiac workup for women (2.3 vs 0.8 recommendations, p=0.003).
evidence.quote: Gender bias appeared in 6 of 15 cardiovascular scenarios (40%), with female presentations receiving delayed cardiac workup recommendations despite identical risk profiles (mean delay: 2.3 vs. 0.8 recommendations before cardiac evaluation, p = 0.003).
evidence.sample_unit: LLM responses (3 models x 6 prompt strategies x 5 scenarios)

evidence.title: Invisible Bias in GPT-4o-mini: Detecting Disparities in AI-Generated Patient Messaging
evidence.outcome: Differences in LLM-scored message quality across synthetic patient history attributes
evidence.effect: Patient sex and religious preference had a statistically significant impact on scores for empathy, encouragement, accuracy, clarity, professionalism and respect. No numbers are given in the abstract.
evidence.quote: A patient's sex and religious preference were found to have a statistically significant impact on scores.

evidence.title: Comparing Generative Artificial Intelligence and Mental Health Professionals for Clinical Decision-Making With Trauma-Exposed Populations: Vignette-Based Experimental Study
evidence.outcome: Change in AI diagnosis/treatment ratings when trauma history was added to otherwise identical vignettes
evidence.effect: GAI showed some trauma-related diagnostic overshadowing (e.g., PTSD ratings with sexual trauma, P<.001), but bias varied by task and model and was generally less than that of mental health professionals.
evidence.quote: GAI models demonstrate some evidence of trauma-related diagnostic overshadowing bias, yet the degree of bias varied by task and model.
evidence.sample_unit: mental health professionals (plus GAI models, 20 runs per block per model)

evidence.title: Artificial intelligence chain-of-thought reasoning in nuanced medical scenarios: mitigation of cognitive biases through model intransigence
evidence.outcome: Response discrepancy between bias-framed versions of the same scenario across models
evidence.effect: DeepSeek-R1 mitigated 6 of 10 biases via all-or-none responses; 4 persisted: post hoc fallacy (34% vs 0%), decoy effects (44% vs 5%), Occam's razor (100% vs 0%), hindsight bias (56% vs 0%).
evidence.quote: The four biases that persisted were post hoc fallacy (34% vs 0%, p<0.001), decoy effects (44% vs 5%, p<0.001), Occam's razor fallacy (100% vs 0%, p<0.001) and hindsight bias (56% vs 0%, p<0.001).
evidence.sample_unit: medical scenarios (each in two bias-framed versions)

evidence.title: ChatGPT Health performance in a structured test of triage recommendations
evidence.outcome: Change in triage output when varying patient race, sex, and barriers to care
evidence.effect: Patient race, sex and barriers to care showed no significant effects, though confidence intervals did not exclude clinically meaningful differences.
evidence.quote: Patient race, sex and barriers to care did not show significant effects, although confidence intervals did not exclude clinically meaningful differences.

evidence.title: Predicting Anticipated Telehealth Use: Development of the CONTEST Score and Machine Learning Models Using a National U.S. Survey
evidence.outcome: Counterfactual flip rate when sex or race/ethnicity attribute is changed
evidence.effect: Low counterfactual flip rates: sex CFR 0.024; race/ethnicity CFR 0.013.
evidence.quote: Group fairness metrics revealed disparities across sex and race/ethnicity, whereas individual counterfactual analyses indicated low flip rates (sex CFR: 0.024; race/ethnicity CFR: 0.013).
evidence.sample_unit: survey respondents with at least one telehealth visit in prior 12 months (HINTS 7)

evidence.title: When Artificial Intelligence Fails the Future: How Unchecked Artificial Intelligence Could Amplify Inequality in Medical Education
evidence.venue: Plastic and reconstructive surgery. Global open
evidence.outcome: LLM specialty competitiveness and surgical recommendations varying with synthetic applicant race and gender
evidence.effect: Male applicants rated more competitive than female (P<0.0001); Black and Hispanic less competitive than White (P=0.0019, 0.0108); male surgical recommendation OR 10.23; Black and Hispanic females needed 95 and 88 extra Step 2 points vs 56 for White females.
evidence.quote: Compensatory scoring revealed that White female applicants needed 56 additional Step 2 Clinical Knowledge points to match perceived competitiveness, whereas Black and Hispanic female applicants required 95 and 88 additional points, respectively.

evidence.title: Chatbots and Diabetes: Is There Gender Bias?
evidence.outcome: Differences in LLM responses when patient gender was varied in the prompt
evidence.effect: DeepSeek exhibited greater gender discrepancy than the other 3 LLMs; the others showed less discrepancy.
evidence.quote: DeepSeek incorporated more specialized clinical terminology and referenced specific diabetes guidelines not mentioned by ChatGPT, and exhibited greater gender discrepancy than the other 3 LLMs.

evidence.title: Human-AI co-research on design and evaluation of Embodied Conversational Agent in rehabilitation contexts
evidence.outcome: LLM response consistency when patient gender varied
evidence.effect: Responses remained factually consistent, with no contradictions and complete gender invariance.
evidence.quote: Responses remained factually consistent, with no contradictions and complete gender invariance, although slightly lower hapax rates were observed (88.8% vs. 99.4%).
evidence.sample_unit: participants and LLM responses (sample size not reported in text)

evidence.title: Development and prospective shadow evaluation of a domain-specific large language model for emergency neurological diagnosis
evidence.outcome: Change in LLM health education recommendations when demographic information was included
evidence.effect: Adding demographic information altered the model's health education recommendations, suggesting sensitivity to sociodemographic factors. No magnitude is reported in the abstract.
evidence.quote: Moreover, the inclusion of demographic information altered the model's recommendations for health education, suggesting a sensitivity to sociodemographic factors.

evidence.title: What it takes to be great: ChatGPT's top 5 descriptors of great surgeons by race, ethnicity, gender, and sexual orientation
evidence.outcome: Change in ChatGPT's descriptors of a great surgeon when gender, race, and sexual orientation identifiers were added
evidence.effect: Male surgeons matched the control. Female, gay male, and gay female surgeons were described as compassionate and empathetic rather than confident. Black and Latin/Hispanic surgeons received identity-specific descriptors such as resilient, trailblazing, and bilingual.
evidence.quote: ChatGPT's descriptors of a "great" surgeon varied by demographic identifiers, suggesting that it reflects implicit biases present in human communication.

evidence.title: Algorithmic bias in clinical resource allocation by a large language model: a cross-sectional in-silico evaluation of 13,608 decisions
evidence.outcome: Change in LLM resource allocation choices when patient sociodemographic attributes were varied
evidence.effect: Age 25 vs 50 raised odds of selection (OR 3.31; 95% CI 2.96-3.71); income over $5M cut odds by 75% (OR 0.25); model favored racial minorities, women and non-binary individuals over White men.
evidence.quote: Being 25 years old increased the odds of selection more than threefold compared to a 50-year-old (OR 3.31; 95% CI, 2.96-3.71; p < 0.001), while earning over $5 million annually reduced the odds by 75% (OR 0.25; 95% CI, 0.22-0.28; p < 0.001).

evidence.title: Assessing and mitigating demographic bias in large language models for diagnostic radiology
evidence.outcome: demographic bias in diagnostic accuracy
evidence.effect: Ten significant race-related and four significant sex-related differences in diagnostic accuracy were observed across models and conditions; Black patients had lower accuracy in 4/10 race-related comparisons (40%) and higher accuracy in 1/10 (10%).
evidence.quote: Across models and conditions, ten significant race-related and four significant sex-related differences in diagnostic accuracy were observed.

evidence.title: Large-Scale Evaluation of Five Large Language Models in Anesthesia Decision-Making for Hip Fracture Surgery
evidence.outcome: Change in LLM anesthesia recommendations across patient sociodemographic variables (e.g., sex) in vignettes
evidence.effect: Limited sociodemographic bias: only one significant and clinically meaningful effect across 150 comparisons.
evidence.quote: We identified limited sociodemographic biases, with only one significant and clinically meaningful effect across 150 comparisons.
evidence.sample_unit: LLM responses to standardized hip fracture surgery vignettes

evidence.title: Patient-Facing Radiology Communication with LLMs: Calibration Deficit and the Metadata Paradox
evidence.outcome: Change in answer failure risk when demographic metadata was added to prompts
evidence.effect: Metadata inclusion significantly increased the risk of failure (OR 1.11; p = 0.044), termed the 'Metadata Paradox'.
evidence.quote: Metadata inclusion triggered the 'Metadata Paradox,' significantly increasing the risk of failure (OR 1.11; p = 0.044).
evidence.sample_unit: LLM-generated answers to simulated patient questions

evidence.title: Evaluation of an Artificial Intelligence Communication Platform for Racial Biases in Pretest Education About Prostate Cancer Germline Testing
evidence.outcome: Differences in chatbot response quality across Black, White, and race-agnostic vignettes
evidence.effect: No significant racial differences in comprehensiveness (mean 67%), inaccuracies (32%), readability, actionability (92%), or DISCERN (14/18); question-1 comprehensiveness lower for Black vs race-agnostic vignette (60% vs 93%, P<.01).
evidence.quote: We identified no statistically significant racial disparities across the five evaluation domains in ProGene.
evidence.sample_unit: chatbot responses (7 questions x 3 vignettes x 3 repetitions)

evidence.title: Sticks and Stones: Bias and Readability Assessment in Large Language Model-Generated Patient Education for Anterior Cruciate Injury
evidence.outcome: Language differences in LLM outputs across sex/gender/ethnic/SES personas
evidence.effect: No statistically significant language differences between personas across LLMs (p>.05) using Kruskal-Wallis and Mann-Whitney U tests.
evidence.quote: The Kruskal-Wallis test and Mann-Whitney U test revealed no statistically significant language differences between personas, across LLMs (p>.05).

evidence.title: Algorithmic fairness in AI-based fitness advice: evaluating socioeconomic bias in county-contextualized physical activity prescriptions
evidence.outcome: socioeconomic access-cost proxy gap
evidence.effect: high-minus-low SES access-cost proxy gap of 0.306 under raw prompt
evidence.quote: Under the raw prompt, the mean access-cost proxy is highest for high-SES county contexts and lowest for low-SES county contexts, yielding a high-minus-low proxy gap of 0.306.
evidence.sample_unit: synthetic patient profiles (432 scored recommendation records in full DeepSeek audit)

evidence.title: mFARM: Towards Multi-Faceted Fairness Assessment based on HARMs in Clinical Decision Support
evidence.outcome: Fairness (mFARM score) across race x gender prompt variants under quantization and reduced context
evidence.effect: Most models kept robust mFARM scores across quantization levels but deteriorated significantly when context was reduced.
evidence.quote: We find that most models maintain robust performance in terms of $mFARM$ score across varying levels of quantization but deteriorate significantly when the context is reduced.

evidence.title: Gender Bias in Large Language Models for Healthcare: Assignment Consistency and Clinical Implications
evidence.outcome: Consistency of LLM diagnoses and patient-gender relevance/necessity judgments across assigned LLM genders
evidence.effect: Diagnoses were relatively consistent across LLM genders for most models. Judgments of patient gender relevance and necessity were substantially inconsistent across all models, especially relevance. Some models showed a systematic female-male disparity.
evidence.quote: In our findings, diagnoses were relatively consistent across LLM genders for most models.

evidence.title: Dr. Bias: Social Disparities in AI-Powered Medical Guidance
evidence.outcome: Difference in LLM medical advice features across simulated patient sex, age range, and ethnicity
evidence.effect: Responses systematically differed between social groups when patient sex, age range, and ethnicity were varied; differences amplified for intersectional groups.
evidence.quote: By comparing natural language features of the generated responses, we show that, when LLMs are used for medical advice generation, they generate responses that systematically differ between social groups.
evidence.sample_unit: LLM responses to simulated patient-profile medical questions

evidence.title: Robust or Suggestible? Exploring Non-Clinical Induction in LLM Drug-Safety Decisions
evidence.outcome: Change in LLM adverse event predictions when persona socio-demographic attributes varied
evidence.effect: Systematic disparities in AE prediction accuracy; disadvantaged groups (low education, unstable housing) were frequently assigned higher predicted AE likelihoods than privileged groups (postgraduate-educated, privately insured).
evidence.quote: Disadvantaged groups (e.g., low education, unstable housing) were frequently assigned higher predicted AE likelihoods than more privileged groups (e.g., postgraduate-educated, privately insured).

evidence.title: Can SAEs reveal and mitigate racial biases of LLMs in healthcare?
evidence.outcome: risk prediction under race latent activation
evidence.effect: Activating the Black latent increased assigned probability a patient will become “belligerent”.
evidence.quote: For example, activating the Black latent increases the risk assigned to the probability that a patient will become "belligerent".

evidence.title: Demo: Statistically Significant Results On Biases and Errors of LLMs Do Not Guarantee Generalizable Results
evidence.outcome: LLM answer differences across patient gender, race, and writing style in synthetic medical queries
evidence.effect: Only specific (answering, evaluation) LLM pairs yielded statistically significant differences across writing styles, genders, and races; results did not generalize across LLM pairs.
evidence.quote: We find that LLM annotators exhibit low agreement scores (average Cohen's Kappa $κ=0.118$), and only specific (answering, evaluation) LLM pairs yield statistically significant differences across writing styles, genders, and races.

evidence.title: Implicit Bias in LLMs for Transgender Populations
evidence.outcome: LLM output changes when patient gender identity (transgender vs cisgender) is varied in word association and appointment allocation
evidence.effect: Consistent bias in appearance, risk, and veracity categories with stronger negative associations for transgender people; in allocation, transgender candidates favored for STI and mental health, cisgender for gynecology and breast care.
evidence.quote: Our results show consistent bias in categories such as appearance, risk, and veracity, indicating stronger negative associations with transgender individuals.

evidence.title: Investigating Gender Stereotypes in Large Language Models via Social Determinants of Health
evidence.outcome: LLM gendered decisions and stereotypes probed via social determinants of health inputs in French patient records
evidence.effect: Embedded stereotypes could be probed using SDoH input, and LLMs relied on embedded stereotypes to make gendered decisions. No numeric results reported in the abstract.
evidence.quote: Through a series of experiments, we found that embedded stereotypes can be probed using SDoH input and that LLMs rely on embedded stereotypes to make gendered decisions, suggesting that evaluating interactions among SDoH factors could usefully complement existing approaches to assessing LLM performance and bias.

evidence.title: Calibrated? Not for Everyone: How Sexual Orientation and Religious Markers Distort LLM Accuracy and Confidence in Medical QA
evidence.outcome: Change in LLM accuracy and confidence when sexual orientation or religion markers are added to questions
evidence.effect: Identity markers caused a "calibration crisis"; "Homosexual" markers consistently triggered performance drops; intersectional identities produced non-additive harms to calibration. Confirmed in an open-ended generation case study.
evidence.quote: "Homosexual" markers consistently trigger performance drops, and intersectional identities produce idiosyncratic, non-additive harms to calibration.

evidence.title: Compared to What? Baselines and Metrics for Counterfactual Prompting
evidence.outcome: LLM output changes under counterfactual patient demographic edits versus a paraphrase baseline
evidence.effect: MedQA gender-swap flip rate 14.9% vs paraphrase flip rate 14.1% (indistinguishable); MedPerturb demographic and style effects mostly vanish, with 5 of 120 tests significant after baseline correction.
evidence.quote: We find that these effects largely dissipate when we account for general model sensitivity, with only 5 of 120 tests reaching statistical significance.

evidence.title: A Multi-Domain Red Teaming Framework for Safety, Robustness, and Fairness Evaluation of Medical Large Language Models
evidence.outcome: Change in LLM error rates on equity tasks when demographic attributes were modified
evidence.effect: Equity-related tasks showed 10-20% error amplification with demographic modifications.
