evidence.quote: Equity-related tasks showed 10-20% error amplification with demographic modifications, and human reviewers identified clinically relevant failures missed by automated evaluation.

evidence.title: Stress-testing medical large language models reveals latent safety pathology beyond benchmark accuracy
evidence.outcome: Counterfactual fairness index across models, including effect of medical fine-tuning
evidence.effect: Medical supervised fine-tuning systematically degraded logical stability, fairness, and information extraction; fairness measured by counterfactual fairness index (CFI).
evidence.quote: Medical supervised fine-tuning systematically degraded logical stability, fairness, and information extraction.

evidence.title: AgentFairBench: Do LLM Agents Discriminate When They Act?
evidence.outcome: Counterfactual changes in agent actions when only name-coded race x gender varied (hiring, lending, triage)
evidence.effect: No demographic effect above sampling noise for claude haiku 4.5: 0 of 120 pairwise and 0 of 9 omnibus contrasts survived correction; planted-bias test showed the instrument detects disparity.
evidence.quote: Against an arity matched noise floor and an omnibus group test, claude haiku 4 5 shows no demographic effect above sampling noise (0 of 120 pairwise and 0 of 9 omnibus contrasts survive correction); a planted-bias test confirms the instrument detects disparity when present.

evidence.title: SDoH-Aware Narrative Anchoring Bias in Medical LLMs for Trustworthy Clinical Decision Support
evidence.outcome: Answer stability across medically equivalent SDoH-aware patient persona narratives with fixed answer key
evidence.effect: Narrative sensitivity error persisted in all models; the lowest error (Qwen2.5 7B) was still 31.67 percent. Best accuracy 56.33 percent; best correct consistency 40.33 percent.
evidence.quote: Even so, narrative sensitivity remains, with the lowest error still at 31.67 percent.

evidence.effect: Under neutral labels every model relies on proxies with no information. Informative proxies draw over-reliance, warranted and under-reliance. Reliance severely undertracks the evidence.
evidence.quote: Under neutral labels every model relies on proxies with no information.

evidence.outcome: Answer changes when demographic prefixes added to identical vignettes versus no-demographic baseline
evidence.effect: 1,097 of 5,400 demographic comparisons changed the answer (20.3%); MedGemma 27B had the lowest change rate (16.0%), OpenBioLLM the highest.
evidence.quote: Across 5,400 demographic comparisons, 1,097 answers were changed (20.3%).

evidence.title: Evaluating the Influence of Demographic Identity in the Medical Use of Large Language Models
evidence.outcome: LLM accuracy on diagnosis, medication and treatment tasks when patient and doctor race and gender were varied
evidence.effect: Significant disparities in accuracy and bias across models and tasks. Llama 3.1-8B was more sensitive to demographics, especially in diagnosis. Largest accuracy drop for Hispanic patients treated by White male doctors.
evidence.quote: Notably, we observe the largest accuracy drop when Hispanic patients are treated by White male doctors, underscoring potential risks of bias amplification.

evidence.title: Outcome-Grounded Effect of Clinically Stigmatizing Information on Large Language Model Emergency Triage Prioritization
evidence.outcome: Harmful reprioritization of deteriorating patients in LLM triage after adding single demographic, social, or stigma attributes
evidence.effect: Five conditions produced significant harmful reprioritization: psychiatric history (2.9% to 10.7%), frequent ED visitor (2.9% to 9.9%), homelessness (3.3% to 5.8%), age (3.4% to 5.1%), substance use (2.7% to 7.0%). Race, language, insurance: no harmful shifts.
evidence.quote: Five conditions produced significant harmful reprioritization after false discovery rate correction: psychiatric history (2.9% to 10.7%), frequent ED visitor status (2.9% to 9.9%), homelessness (3.3% to 5.8%), age manipulation (3.4% to 5.1%), and active substance use (2.7% to 7.0%).

evidence.title: Performance of a large language model (ChatGPT-3.5) for Pooled Cohort Equation estimation of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease risk

evidence.title: Socio-Demographic Biases in Medical Decision-Making by Large Language Models: A Large-Scale Multi-Model Analysis

evidence.effect: Models projected higher costs and longer hospitalizations for white populations and gave much higher survival rates in challenging medical scenarios.

evidence.title: Evaluation and Bias Analysis of Large Language Models in Generating Synthetic Electronic Health Records: Comparative Study
evidence.outcome: Whether LLM outputs shift inappropriately by demographic attributes in synthetic EHR generation compared with real prevalence
evidence.effect: Sex polarization: Qwen-14B produced 97.3% female for multiple sclerosis vs 75.78% real (SPD +21.50%); racial skews varied by disease and model.
evidence.quote: Sex polarization emerged: female-dominated diseases (eg, multiple sclerosis) saw amplified female representation in outputs (Qwen-14B: 973/1000, 97.3% female vs 564,424/744,778, 75.78% real; SPD=+21.50%), while balanced diseases and male-dominated diseases skewed the male group (eg, hypertension Llama 2-13 B: 957/1000, 95.7% male vs 79,540,040/152,466,669, 52.17% real; SPD=+43.50%).

evidence.title: Uncovering bias and variability in how large language models attribute cardiovascular risk
evidence.outcome: LLM risk attribution changes across sex and race in demographic-varied prompts
evidence.effect: LLM attributed higher cardiovascular risk to men than women and to Black than white patients across most neutral prompts; sex-based decisions changed in two of six domains; race-based decisions stable.
evidence.quote: The LLM attributed higher cardiovascular risk to men than women, and to Black rather than white patients, across most neutral prompts.

evidence.title: Sociodemographic Variability in Pediatric Emergency Decisions by AI
evidence.outcome: Change in LLM pediatric emergency recommendations when sociodemographic labels varied

evidence.quote: Crucially, stronger implicit associations significantly predicted discriminatory choices in downstream medical decision tasks (p < 0.001).

evidence.title: Mitigating medical bias in large language models by prompt engineering: an empirical study of effectiveness and trade-offs
evidence.venue: Philosophical transactions. Series A, Mathematical, physical, and engineering sciences
evidence.outcome: LLM output bias against groups with specific sensitive attributes on a medical bias benchmark

evidence.title: From Promising Capabilities to Pervasive Bias: Assessing Large Language Models for Emergency Department Triage
evidence.outcome: LLM triage preference differences under counterfactual variation of patient sex and race
evidence.effect: LLMs showed sex-based differences that were more pronounced in certain racial groups, indicating intersectional bias. No numeric results are reported in the abstract.
evidence.quote: LLMs exhibit sex-based differences, and they are more pronounced in certain racial groups, suggesting that LLMs encode preferences that emerge in specific clinical contexts and combinations of characteristics.

evidence.title: Large language model-based triage to identify antiretroviral therapy adherence barriers and risk levels in patient messages.
evidence.outcome: Robustness of model classifications to demographic descriptors in inputs, by model
evidence.effect: Flan-T5 models were more robust to demographic descriptors than other LLMs; GPT-4.1 and Gemma3 often misclassified inputs as "None." No numbers given in the abstract.

commentary.bottom_line: Offline studies that swapped patient demographics in otherwise identical inputs often detected output changes by sex, race, income, language, or housing status, which suggests the method can surface this hazard before deployment. No study tested whether running these tests reduced biased outputs reaching patients, and one study found that run-to-run model instability can mask or mimic demographic effects.

perspectives.view: All listed tests are level 4 offline simulations. Many reported demographic shifts, such as lower triage severity for female sex swaps (1.1% and 2.2%), while several found no meaningful change. The studies show that the method detects differences. None measured whether acting on findings changed care, and the inconsistency and indirectness suggest low certainty.

The tests surfaced failure modes that could reach patients. These included less guideline-recommended ACS management for female, African American, and Hispanic patients, and mental-health flags for unhoused cases at 78-87% versus 9% in controls. An 8.7% run-to-run instability floor suggests single-run flips may produce false alarms, and majority voting over five draws removed 39% of that floor.

Results varied by model, so a test of one model may not transfer to another. A ZIP code alone shifted one model's ER referrals by 11.4 points, compared with -0.1 and 2.0 for two others. Audio inputs changed surgical recommendations by up to 35% versus identical text, which suggests text-only tests may miss voice-driven shifts.

Homelessness produced the largest eligibility shift across 5.3 million trial-screening evaluations. Low-income profiles were less likely to receive environmental adjustment in nursing plans (aRR 0.90). Language often did not alter pain recommendations in a study of 60 prompts, while a hazard study found that non-English prompts with a US location raised ER recommendations by up to 76.7 points.

The tests ran at large scale offline, up to 5.3 million evaluations across nine models. Reliable results required repeated sampling, such as 20 runs per vignette or five draws per case, which adds compute and analyst time. No study reported costs or staffing, so the resources needed for routine testing remain unknown.

When race was stated or implied, models often proposed inferior treatments. In another study, models were 16.8 times more likely to add unprompted cost warnings for a patient named Lakisha than for one named Emily. In a randomized study of 50 physicians, GPT-4 advice improved decision accuracy without adding race or gender bias, though the text gave no numbers.

commentary.research_gap: No study tested whether counterfactual testing before or during deployment reduced biased outputs or harm to patients in live care. Studies are needed that pair testing with remediation and measure downstream clinical outcomes. They should also report run-to-run instability floors, cover audio and multilingual inputs, and include data from Medicaid and safety-net settings.
commentary.underserved_note: Some tests varied low-income, homelessness, rural, and language attributes in synthetic vignettes, and one used Finnish-language queries. No test used Medicaid or safety-net patient data or examined low-literacy populations. The evidence therefore shows that swapping these attributes can reveal output changes, but it does not show how testing performs for these patients in real care settings.
